problem: Language-to-Reward (L2R) methods generate rewards from task text without visually inspecting how the learned policy physically fails, so rewards lack physical grounding; direct VLA/LLM control avoids this but requires querying a large model at every step, which is slow.
motivation: Continuous robot control needs low-latency, lightweight policies, yet foundation models offer the semantic and visual reasoning that long-horizon sparse-reward tasks need. Using foundation models only at training time to refine rewards from visual failure evidence could combine both.
key_idea: Use an LLM to write executable reward code for a hierarchical RL policy, and when training stagnates let a frozen VLM diagnose failed rollout frames so the LLM rewrites and densifies the reward, so that deployment needs only the small policy.
insight: Visual failure diagnosis lets the reward encode geometric constraints such as wall openings or grasp order that text alone misses. The maze case study shows a static LLM reward getting trapped at a wall, while the VLM-informed penalty routes the agent through the opening. Splitting the work into a VLM critic and an LLM coder is preferred over a single VLM, which hallucinated blocks and made dimension errors in reward code (qualitative only, no numeric ablation). Confining foundation models to training gives about 500 Hz control against about 50 Hz for a VLA.
method: Initial reward synthesis: an LLM (llama-3.3-70b) turns the task instruction and generic environment APIs into an executable Python reward R_H^(0), a weighted sum of residual distance and heuristic terms for the high-level policy.
Hierarchical RL policy: a two-level SAC hierarchy of 3-layer, 512-unit MLPs; the high level proposes subgoals every k steps, the low level is trained with a subgoal-distance penalty.
Event-triggered stagnation detector: monitors the moving-average success rate and fires when its gradient is about 0 and it is below a threshold.
VLM visual critic: a frozen VLM (llama-4-scout-17b) gets frames of the latest failed trajectory plus the task and returns a 2-sentence physical failure diagnosis.

Reward rewriting and relabeling: the LLM rewrites the reward code from the task, previous reward and VLM feedback to add dense penalties; high-level replay transitions are relabeled with the current reward.
Deployment: only the MLP hierarchy runs, with no LLM or VLM queries.

setting.backbone: Hierarchical SAC MLP policies (3 layers x 512) trained from scratch; llama-3.3-70b (LLM, frozen) and llama-4-scout-17b (VLM, frozen) used only at training time
setting.training_data: Online RL in simulation with LLM/VLM-synthesized rewards; a single demonstration with an imitation objective at the low level for pick-and-place and kitchen; no demos for maze
setting.observation: Low-dimensional state vectors (gripper/object positions, velocities, maze array); rendered frames for the VLM critic during training only; real robot uses a RealSense D435 depth camera
setting.action_space: Continuous 4-D end-effector offsets [dx,dy,dz,gripper] for the low level; subgoals from the high level
setting.simulator: MuJoCo-based Fetch-style maze, pick-and-place and bin environments; D4RL Franka Kitchen
setting.privileged: none at deployment; the reward code uses environment APIs such as goal position, door and bin positions during training

numbers.backbone: Hierarchical SAC MLP; llama-3.3-70b + llama-4-scout-17b during training
numbers.extra: 1 demonstration for the low level; comparison to SmolVLA fine-tuned on 100 demos (29% SR, 50 Hz)
numbers.evidence: Fig. 1 caption / RQ5: 'VGRS restricts foundation models to training and deploys a lightweight policy, achieving 81% success at approx 500 Hz'

numbers.backbone: Hierarchical SAC MLP, trained in simulation
numbers.extra: sim-to-real; loop capped at 20 Hz by the SDK; L2R baseline failed
numbers.evidence: RQ6: 'average success rate of 60% (variance 0.07) on pick-and-place'

numbers.backbone: Hierarchical SAC MLP, trained in simulation

numbers_note: Simulation results for maze, bin and kitchen are only in learning-curve figures (no tables); the abstract claims success above 55% on long-horizon tasks. The 81% pick-and-place figure comes from the figure caption and text.
results: VGRS outperforms L2R, SAGA, RAPS, HAC, HIER and DAC on pick-and-place, bin and kitchen, and is competitive on maze. It reaches 81% on pick-and-place at about 500 Hz versus 29% at 50 Hz for a fine-tuned SmolVLA. On a real Dobot arm it gets 60% on pick-and-place and 60% on bin, where L2R failed.
limitations: The VLM diagnosis from sparse frames may be insufficient for occluded scenes or tasks needing tactile information.
The compiled policy cannot follow new zero-shot instructions without retraining.
Evaluation is on a few simple simulated tasks and the ablations are qualitative, with no numeric comparison of VLM-only versus VLM+LLM.
